lesson_title: The Letter Home: How Migration Reshapes Two Places at Once
hook_text: Follow the money sent home at month end and you can explain every migration on the map.
clip_script: Stand at a taxi rank on a Monday morning. Some passengers ride twenty minutes to work — that is not migration, just the daily loop. But some carry everything they own, headed for a city they have never seen. Residence is about to change. THAT is migration. Now here is the object that explains everything it causes: the money sent home at month end. Once a letter with notes folded inside, now a banking app. Millions of transfers, every month — Gauteng to the Eastern Cape, South Africa to Zimbabwe and Lesotho. Follow one. It lands in a village as groceries, school shoes, a grandmother's electricity — often the household's main income. But look around that village at what is missing: the working-age adults. Fields nobody ploughs. Children raised by grandparents. The village gains money and loses its strongest people — both at once. Now trace the money back to the city. The city gained a worker: the builder from Lusikisiki, the nurse from Harare, the shopkeeper from Mogadishu. Cities are built by exactly such people. But it also strains — more arrivals than houses, more job-seekers than jobs. Four boxes: village gains, village loses, city gains, city strains. Fill them, and you understand migration.
visual_style: A taxi rank at dawn; an animated money transfer flying from a city skyline to a rural homestead and splitting into groceries and school shoes; a fading silhouette of absent adults; four boxes stamping onto screen.
pacing: Observational open, steady tracing of the money both ways, crisp four-box landing.
